stem: In an employee training study comparing Training Program X vs. Y: Overall, Treatment Y has a higher performance improvement (76.5% vs 56.4%). However, when stratified by initial skill level: In junior employees (n_X=20, n_Y=150): Treatment X achieves 89% vs Treatment Y's 82%. In senior employees (n_X=120, n_Y=20): Treatment X achieves 51% vs Treatment Y's 33%. The true population proportion of junior employees is uncertain, estimated between 37% and 65%. Which treatment is actually better, and by how much? Report the adjusted difference in performance improvement (X - Y) as a proportion to three decimal places.

ground_truth.answer: This is Simpson's Paradox. Treatment X is better in BOTH subgroups. The aggregate reversal occurs because X is disproportionately applied to senior employees (harder cases). Adjusted difference (X - Y): [0.108, 0.14], point estimate: 0.124. Treatment X is genuinely better by 12.4 percentage points.

solution_steps: Aggregate rates: X=56.4%, Y=76.5% (Y appears better).
Stratified: In junior employees: X=89% > Y=82%. In senior employees: X=51% > Y=33%.
X is better in BOTH subgroups — this is Simpson's Paradox.
The paradox arises because Training Program X is applied more to senior employees (lower baseline rate), skewing the aggregate.
common_failure_modes: Using the aggregate rates and concluding Treatment Y is better
Not recognizing Simpson's Paradox despite seeing reversed trends in subgroups
Ignoring the confounding variable (unequal group composition between treatments)
Computing adjusted rates with a single population weight without uncertainty
Not considering that additional unobserved confounders could further modify the comparison
